page_title: Write a time-series database engine from scratch

sources.entry: Write a time-series database engine from scratch

summary.title: Write a time-series database engine from scratch
summary.one_liner: You learn how a lightweight time-series storage engine can be built in Go using time-partitioned memory and disk segments, a WAL, mmap-ed files, and Gorilla-style delta-of-delta and XOR compression.
keywords: build a time series database in go
lsm tree vs time series storage
takeaways: Time-series data is append-only, ordered by time, read in bulk over time ranges, and often high-cardinality, which shapes storage design.
Partitioning data by time lets memory partitions take writes (with a WAL for durability) while older partitions become read-only files on disk.
Storing each partition in one mmap-ed file grouped by metric improves locality and avoids one file per metric.
Gorilla-style encoding compresses timestamps with delta-of-delta (zeros for regular intervals) and floats with XOR, which works best when data is written at regular intervals.
The author notes drawbacks: per-metric index metadata stays on the heap, so heap use grows linearly with the number of metrics in a partition.
summary.summary: The author describes writing tstorage, a lightweight pure-Go time-series storage engine for local disks, motivated by a load testing tool whose heap usage grew over time. The post explains time-series characteristics (append-only, time-ordered, bulk reads, high cardinality) and why LevelDB/LSM designs were considered. It then covers the time-partitioned data model, memory partitions with WAL and out-of-order handling, disk partitions with a single mmap-ed data file and JSON metadata index, and Gorilla-based encoding using delta-of-delta for timestamps and XOR for values, with worked examples. It closes with the drawbacks of keeping index metadata on the heap.
